title: Malaysia | AMLA and BNM AML/CFT/CPF and TFS Compliance
tagline: Apply Malaysia's amended AMLA and Bank Negara Malaysia's AML/CFT/CPF and TFS rules with confidence at a conventional bank.
description:
This quest teaches the anti-money laundering, counter-terrorism financing and counter-proliferation financing rules that apply to conventional banks in Malaysia. It is based on the **Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 (AMLA)** as amended by **Act A1761**, in force from 1 March 2026, and on **Bank Negara Malaysia's** policy document on AML/CFT/CPF and Targeted Financial Sanctions for Financial Institutions, effective 6 February 2024.

Section 19 of AMLA makes ongoing employee training part of every reporting institution's compliance programme, and BNM requires regular training with refreshers, pitched to each role, with customer-facing staff trained before they deal with customers. Since March 2026 key AMLA duties also bind directors, officers and employees personally. This quest supports that duty for branch, onboarding, operations, screening and compliance staff and their managers.

In five stages you join the compliance team of a fictional Malaysian bank: the law, customer due diligence, suspicious transaction reporting, targeted financial sanctions and the bank's programme.

The quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own AML/CFT/CPF policies and procedures; always follow them and the latest BNM requirements.
audience: Tellers, branch and account-opening staff at conventional banks in Malaysia who carry out CDD and handle cash
Relationship managers in retail, SME and corporate banking who onboard customers and spot unusual activity
Compliance, AML monitoring and sanctions screening staff who review alerts, submit reports to FIED and handle name matches
Branch compliance officers, line managers and senior managers who approve higher-risk relationships
Directors, internal auditors and risk managers who oversee or test the bank's AML/CFT/CPF programme
outcomes: Explain how AMLA, Act A1761 and BNM's AML/CFT/CPF and TFS policy document fit together, and which duties now bind you personally
Apply BNM's CDD, beneficial ownership, enhanced CDD and PEP requirements to real onboarding decisions
Escalate suspicion through the internal chain so the Compliance Officer can report promptly to FIED, and avoid tipping off
Apply cash threshold reporting and record-keeping rules, including the six-year minimum retention period
Screen, freeze, reject and report under Malaysia's targeted financial sanctions on terrorism and proliferation financing
Describe the roles of the board, senior management and Compliance Officer, the training and audit duties, and BNM's enforcement tools

sessions.title: The Rulebook: AMLA, Act A1761 and BNM's Policy Document
sessions.summary: Map Malaysia's AML/CFT/CPF framework: AMLA as amended by Act A1761, BNM and FIED, the policy document's S and G paragraphs, personal duties and penalties.

cards.title: Day one at Seri Merbau Bank
cards.setting: Compliance floor, Seri Merbau Bank head office, KL Sentral. 9:05 am, a Monday in March 2026.

lines.text: Your badge says AML/CFT/CPF Officer. Your mission: keep dirty money, terrorist funds and proliferation money out of Seri Merbau Bank.
Selamat datang! I'm Nurul, the bank's Compliance Officer for AML/CFT/CPF. Five stages lie ahead, and BNM examiners are due before year end.
(video call from Penang) Daniel here, branch compliance. A customer asked our teller, very casually, whether the bank 'tells the government' about his deposits. She froze.
And the amended AMLA came into force on 1 March. Half the branch thinks it only changed the Act's name.
My team in JB asks a simpler question: if something goes wrong, is it the bank's problem or ours?
Since this month, the honest answer is: both. Before you judge a single deposit, you need the map. Which law, which rule, and who does what.
Stage one is the Statute Gate. Ready to read the rulebook the way a BNM examiner does?

scenes.heading: The Act sets the base
scenes.narration: It starts with the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, known as AMLA. It creates the money laundering offence and the reporting, due diligence, record-keeping and compliance programme duties of reporting institutions such as your bank.

scenes.heading: Act A1761 rewires it
scenes.narration: Act A1761 amended AMLA from 1 March 2026. It adds restricted activity financing, meaning proliferation financing, renames the Act, and extends key duties to the directors, officers and employees of reporting institutions personally.

scenes.heading: BNM is the competent authority
scenes.narration: Bank Negara Malaysia administers AMLA. Its Financial Intelligence and Enforcement Department, FIED, is Malaysia's financial intelligence unit and receives suspicious transaction reports and cash threshold reports.

scenes.heading: The policy document adds detail
scenes.narration: BNM's policy document on AML/CFT/CPF and Targeted Financial Sanctions for Financial Institutions took effect on 6 February 2024. Paragraphs marked S are binding standards; paragraphs marked G are guidance.

scenes.heading: Your bank closes the loop
scenes.narration: Finally, your board approves the bank's AML/CFT/CPF policies and senior management turns them into procedures. That is the layer you apply every day, and it must sit inside the layers above.

cards.title: From statute to your desk
cards.caption: Each layer must stay inside the one above it. When a bank procedure is looser than the policy document, the policy document wins.

items.label: AMLA 2001, as amended by Act A1761
items.detail: Offences, reporting, CDD, records, compliance programme, sanctions powers and enforcement.

items.label: Orders under AMLA
items.detail: Domestic List declarations and UN sanctions measures given effect in Malaysian law.

items.detail: Binding S standards and G guidance on risk, CDD, reporting, records and TFS.

items.label: Bank's board-approved policy
items.detail: How Seri Merbau Bank applies the law and the policy document to its risks.

items.label: Procedures and system rules
items.detail: The forms, checklists and screening settings you use on every case.

cards.title: Who does what in Malaysia
cards.prompt: Match each body to its main AML/CFT/CPF role for a bank.

pairs.right: Competent authority under AMLA and supervisor of banks: issues the policy document, examines and takes enforcement action.
Financial intelligence unit: receives STRs, cash threshold reports and TFS match reports from reporting institutions.
Declares specified entities on the Domestic List and authorises any dealing with funds frozen under it.
Authorises dealings with, and exemptions for, funds frozen under the proliferation financing sanctions.
Receives the bank's immediate report, alongside FIED, when it holds funds of a terrorism-related specified entity.
Approves AML/CFT/CPF policies and keeps oversight of the whole programme.

cards.question: A paragraph in BNM's policy document is marked G. What does that mean for Seri Merbau Bank?
options: It is guidance: a recommended way of meeting the standards, not a binding requirement on its own
It is a general standard that applies to every reporting institution without exception
It applies only to groups of companies with foreign branches
It must be followed exactly, and any departure is an offence under AMLA
cards.explanation: The policy document marks binding standards with S and guidance with G. Paragraph 9.1 says enforcement or supervisory action can follow breaches of S provisions. G paragraphs show good ways to comply, so departing from them needs a sound reason, but they are not standards in themselves.

cards.title: What Act A1761 changed in March 2026
cards.body:
Act A1761 was gazetted on 14 May 2025 and brought into force on 1 March 2026. For bank staff, five changes matter most:

- **New name and new offence.** The Act now also covers *restricted activity financing*, that is financing linked to weapons of mass destruction and their delivery, with an offence in new section 66H.
- **Personal duties.** Record keeping (s13), CDD (s16), record retention (s17) and the compliance programme (s19) now bind the reporting institution **or its director, officer or employee**. Breaching ss16 or 19 can bring a fine of up to RM1 million.
- **BNM can specify more.** BNM may issue directions, guidelines and other instruments to banks and their people, and they must comply.
- **Administrative action.** New section 83B lets BNM direct compliance, reprimand, issue a public statement or impose a monetary penalty of up to RM1 million, after written notice and a chance to respond.
- **Court orders and publicity.** BNM can seek orders, including removing a CEO, director or manager, and may publish its actions.

cards.title: Where does this rule live?
cards.prompt: Sort each rule into the layer where it is set.

items.text: Money laundering offence with up to 15 years' imprisonment
Offence of tipping off about a suspicious transaction report
Offence of structuring transactions to avoid reporting
Cash threshold report submitted within five working days
Delayed verification may not exceed ten working days
FIED told of a new Compliance Officer within ten working days
How many days the Compliance Officer has to review an internal report
Which internal form a teller uses to raise a concern

cards.title: What breaches can cost under AMLA
cards.caption: Figures from AMLA as amended by Act A1761. Your bank's disciplinary rules apply on top of these.

items.label: Money laundering (s4)
items.detail: Maximum prison term, plus a fine of at least five times the proceeds or RM5 million, whichever is higher.

items.label: Tipping off (s14A)
items.detail: Maximum fine or prison term, or both, for disclosing a report or related information.

items.label: CDD or programme breach
items.detail: Maximum fine for breaching ss16 or 19, now for the bank or its director, officer or employee.

items.label: Administrative penalty (s83B)
items.detail: Maximum monetary penalty BNM may impose, in proportion to the gravity of the breach.

cards.title: Real case: SME Bank and staff awareness (BNM, 2025)
cards.body:
On 20 November 2025 BNM imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM460,000** on Small Medium Enterprise Development Bank Malaysia Berhad for failing to submit suspicious transaction reports promptly, a requirement in paragraph 22.1.1 of the policy document then in force.

BNM found that the bank did not report promptly on suspicious activity by several customers. Its public notice put the breach down to **inadequate staff awareness** of STR requirements. The bank's remedies included stronger internal AML/CFT policies and better training for relevant staff. In setting the penalty BNM weighed the severity of the breach, the lack of reasonable care, the bank's controls and its past record.

**The lesson for you:** a training gap is not a soft issue. When staff do not know what to escalate, the bank misses its reporting duty, and BNM treats that as a breach with a price tag.

cards.title: 'Isn't that compliance's job?'
cards.setting: Video call between head office and Johor Bahru, 4:30 pm.

lines.text: Honest question from my RMs: CDD and reporting are the Compliance Officer's job, right? We sell, compliance checks.
(joining from the boardroom) That was never quite true, Kavitha. And since 1 March the Act itself names directors, officers and employees in sections 16 and 19.
BNM's policy document already said staff must be told they can be held personally liable. Paragraph 9.1 allows action against directors, officers and employees too.
So if one of my RMs skips a beneficial owner check to close a deal...
Then the bank has a problem, and the RM may have one too. Let's test that with a real-looking case.

cards.title: The VIP who is 'in a hurry'
cards.situation: A long-standing corporate client tells Kavitha's newest RM, Hafiz, that he needs a second company account opened today for a property deal. He promises the shareholder list 'next week' and says the previous RM never asked for it. The deal is worth a lot of fee income, and Hafiz's manager is on leave. What should Hafiz do?

choices.text: Open the account today and chase the shareholder list next week; the client is well known to the bank.
choices.outcome: Risky. Identifying beneficial owners is part of CDD, and delayed verification is only allowed for low-risk cases with no suspicion, within strict limits. Under the amended AMLA, Hafiz himself can breach the CDD duty.

choices.text: Explain that the bank must complete CDD, including the owners, before opening, and refer any exception request to compliance.
choices.outcome: Best. Hafiz applies the bank's procedure, does not accuse the client of anything, and lets compliance decide whether any permitted flexibility applies. If the client refuses or the story keeps changing, compliance can consider an STR.

choices.text: Open the account but block it until the documents arrive, without telling compliance.
choices.outcome: Partly sensible, but Hafiz is improvising a control the bank has not approved. Any delayed verification must follow the bank's documented risk procedures, not a private arrangement.

choices.text: Ask a colleague to open it under their login so Hafiz is not responsible.
choices.outcome: Poor. It hides who acted, breaks the bank's controls and does nothing to meet the CDD duty. It could also be seen as an attempt to evade personal accountability.

cards.back: A person or business listed in AMLA's First Schedule, such as a licensed bank, that must meet AMLA's reporting, CDD, record-keeping and compliance programme duties.
The authority that administers AMLA's reporting regime. For banks this is Bank Negara Malaysia, acting through FIED.
A term taken from the Strategic Trade Act 2010, linked to weapons of mass destruction. Financing it is an offence under new section 66H.
Under the amended AMLA, a person who commits, attempts or facilitates a restricted activity, or is designated a prohibited end-user under the Strategic Trade Act.
A person or group on the Domestic List declared by the Minister of Home Affairs, or on the UN terrorism-related lists, whose funds must be frozen.
In BNM's policy document, S marks a binding standard and G marks guidance on how to comply.

items.detail: Act 613 creates the money laundering offence and reporting institution duties.

items.detail: BNM's AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for FIs document adds proliferation financing.

cards.question: Since 1 March 2026, who can commit an offence by breaching the CDD duty in section 16 of AMLA?
options: Only the reporting institution itself, as a body corporate
The reporting institution, or its director, officer or employee
Only the Compliance Officer named to FIED
Only directors who sit on the board risk committee
cards.explanation: Act A1761 inserted 'or the director, officer or employee of the reporting institution' into section 16 and added a fine of up to RM1 million for breaches. The Compliance Officer has key duties, but CDD is not his or hers alone.

cards.title: Reading a BNM paragraph reference
cards.body:
BNM numbers its policy document in a way you will meet in every audit report and enforcement notice:

- **14A** is CDD for banking and deposit-taking institutions; 14B to 14D cover other sectors, so ignore them at a bank.
- **22** is suspicious transaction reports, **21** cash threshold reports, **24** record keeping.
- **27, 28 and 29** are targeted financial sanctions on terrorism financing, proliferation financing and other UN regimes.
- **11.6** is employee training.

Check the S or G marker in the margin before you call something mandatory.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: AMLA, as amended by Act A1761 from 1 March 2026, is the base law; BNM's AML/CFT/CPF and TFS policy document sets the detailed rules for banks.
BNM is the competent authority; its FIED is the financial intelligence unit that receives STRs, cash threshold reports and TFS reports.
Act A1761 added restricted activity (proliferation) financing and made key duties bind directors, officers and employees personally.
S paragraphs are binding standards; G paragraphs are guidance. Enforcement can follow breaches of S paragraphs.
BNM can now impose administrative penalties of up to RM1 million, reprimand, publish and seek court orders.

cards.prompt: Think of one task you do every week that touches a customer, an account or a payment. Which AMLA duty does it serve, and what would change for you personally now that the Act names employees?

quiz.question: Which body is Malaysia's financial intelligence unit that receives suspicious transaction reports from banks?
options: The Securities Commission Malaysia's investigation and enforcement division in Kuala Lumpur
BNM's Financial Intelligence and Enforcement Department
The Royal Malaysia Police commercial crime unit
The Companies Commission of Malaysia
quiz.explanation: BNM is the competent authority under AMLA, and its FIED receives STRs and cash threshold reports. The police and other agencies act on intelligence but are not where banks file STRs.

quiz.question: From what date did the amendments made by Act A1761 to AMLA come into force?
options: 6 February 2024
1 January 2026
1 March 2026
quiz.explanation: Act A1761 was gazetted on 14 May 2025 and came into force on 1 March 2026. 6 February 2024 is when BNM's AML/CFT/CPF and TFS policy document took effect.

quiz.question: What new kind of financing did Act A1761 bring into AMLA, alongside money laundering and terrorism financing?
options: Restricted activity financing, linked to weapons of mass destruction
Online gambling financing, linked to illegal betting sites
Tax evasion financing, linked to offshore structures and undeclared overseas income
Wildlife trade financing, linked to protected species
quiz.explanation: Act A1761 added restricted activity financing, defined by reference to the Strategic Trade Act 2010, with an offence in new section 66H. The Act's name now includes Anti-Restricted Activity Financing.

quiz.question: A relationship manager tells a new colleague: 'Under AMLA only the bank can be liable for CDD failures, never us.' Since March 2026, is she right?
options: Yes: CDD duties remain with the reporting institution as a body corporate only
Yes, unless the employee is the named Compliance Officer at head office
No: section 16 now applies to the bank or its director, officer or employee
No, but only directors can be fined, not ordinary employees
quiz.explanation: Act A1761 extended section 16 to directors, officers and employees, with a fine of up to RM1 million for breaches. BNM's policy document already required staff to be told they may be personally liable.

quiz.question: What is the maximum prison term for the money laundering offence under section 4 of AMLA?
options: Five years
Seven years
Fifteen years
Twenty years
quiz.explanation: Section 4 carries imprisonment of up to fifteen years plus a fine of at least five times the proceeds or RM5 million, whichever is higher. Five years is the maximum for tipping off.

quiz.question: Kavitha reads paragraph 11.6.6 of BNM's policy document and sees a G in the margin. How should she treat it?
options: As guidance on a good way to comply, not a binding standard on its own
As a binding standard whose breach is an offence under section 86
As a rule that applies only to development financial institutions, not banks
As a requirement that applies only to the board of directors
quiz.explanation: S marks standards and G marks guidance. Paragraph 9.1 ties enforcement to S provisions. G paragraphs still show what BNM considers good practice.

quiz.question: Under new section 83B of AMLA, which of these may BNM do after giving written notice and a chance to respond?
options: Imprison an employee for up to three years
Revoke a bank's licence without any court process
Seize a director's personal assets
Impose a monetary penalty of up to RM1 million
quiz.explanation: Section 83B allows directions, monetary penalties up to RM1 million, reprimands or public statements, and remedial requirements. Prison is a criminal penalty that only a court can impose.

quiz.question: A branch manager says the bank's procedure lets tellers delay verification for up to twenty working days for busy customers. BNM's policy document says ten. Which applies?
options: The bank's twenty days, because the board approved the procedure
The policy document's ten working days, because bank procedures must sit within it
Whichever period the branch manager considers reasonable in the circumstances of each case
Neither, because delayed verification is not allowed at all
quiz.explanation: The bank's policies and procedures must comply with the policy document. Paragraph 14A.10.7 caps 'reasonably practicable' at ten working days unless BNM specifies otherwise.

quiz.question: BNM imposed RM460,000 on SME Bank in 2025 for late STRs. What root cause did BNM's notice identify?
options: Inadequate staff awareness of STR-related requirements
A failed upgrade to the bank's transaction monitoring system
Deliberate concealment of reports by senior management
A shortage of staff in the bank's compliance team
quiz.explanation: BNM's notice attributed the breach to inadequate staff awareness and noted the bank enhanced its policies and staff training. That is why training is a programme requirement, not an extra.

quiz.question: Farid tells a new joiner that the Minister of Home Affairs and the Strategic Trade Controller both play roles in Malaysia's sanctions regime. Which statement is accurate?
options: The Controller declares the Domestic List, while the Minister handles all PF exemptions and dealings
Both bodies receive STRs directly from banks instead of FIED
The Minister declares the Domestic List; the Controller authorises dealings in PF-frozen funds
Both bodies are departments within Bank Negara Malaysia
quiz.explanation: The Domestic List is declared by the Minister of Home Affairs under section 66B, and the Minister authorises dealings with funds frozen under it. For proliferation financing, BNM's policy document points to the Strategic Trade Controller.

sessions.title: Know Your Customer: Risk, CDD, Beneficial Owners, EDD and PEPs
sessions.summary: Apply BNM's risk-based approach and paragraph 14A CDD rules: triggers, data, verification, the beneficial owner cascade, enhanced CDD, PEPs, higher-risk countries and reliance.
objectives: Identify when CDD is required and what standard CDD collects
Apply the beneficial owner cascade to companies and trusts
Decide when enhanced CDD applies and what it requires, including for PEPs
Explain the limits on delayed verification and reliance on third parties

cards.title: Layers in Johor Bahru
cards.setting: Seri Merbau Bank, Johor Bahru business centre. 10:20 am.

lines.text: Big one today: Tebrau Freight Sdn Bhd wants a current account and trade lines. Lots of business through the port.
Shareholders: a Malaysian individual with 30 per cent, and a Labuan company with 70 per cent. The Labuan company's owners are 'confidential', says their lawyer.
(on speaker) And the directors?
One director mentioned, proudly, that his wife's father is a senior state government official.
So we have a hidden owner, a possible PEP family member and a cash-heavy port business. Which box do we tick first?
No box first. Risk first. Stage two is the Onboarding Hall: who we must identify, how deep we go, and when we stop.

cards.title: The risk-based approach to knowing your customer

scenes.heading: Start with risk
scenes.narration: BNM expects every bank to identify and assess its money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing risks, guided by Malaysia's National Risk Assessment, and to scale its controls to those risks.

scenes.heading: Profile each customer
scenes.narration: Each customer gets a risk rating. The profile weighs the type of customer, the countries involved, the products and channels used, such as cash or non face-to-face, and any other sign of higher risk.

scenes.heading: Do the CDD
scenes.narration: Identify and verify the customer, anyone acting for them and the beneficial owners, and understand the purpose of the relationship.

scenes.heading: Go deeper where risk is higher
scenes.narration: Higher risk means enhanced CDD: more information, source of wealth or funds, and senior management approval before the relationship starts or continues.

scenes.heading: Keep watching
scenes.narration: CDD never ends at account opening. Ongoing due diligence checks that transactions fit the profile and that records stay up to date, more often for higher-risk customers.

cards.title: When a bank must carry out CDD (paragraph 14A.1)
cards.caption: Sanctions screening applies to every customer and transaction regardless of these thresholds.

items.label: Establishing a business relationship
items.detail: Opening an account or any new relationship.

items.label: Money-changing, wire transfers, e-money
items.detail: Specific CDD measures apply under paragraph 14A.11.

items.label: Occasional transactions of RM25,000 or more
items.detail: Including several transactions in a day that appear linked.

items.label: Cash transactions of RM25,000 or more
items.detail: Physical cash, whichever product it touches.

items.label: Any suspicion of ML/TF/PF
items.detail: Regardless of amount.

items.label: Doubt about earlier CDD information
items.detail: When previously obtained data looks wrong or incomplete.

cards.title: Finding the beneficial owner of a company (paragraph 14A.9.6)
cards.caption: Stop at the first step that identifies a beneficial owner. Only natural persons can be ultimate beneficial owners.

items.label: Step 1: ownership
items.detail: Identify natural persons with a controlling ownership interest; at minimum directors, partners and shareholders with more than 25% equity.

items.label: Step 2: control by other means
items.detail: If ownership leaves doubt, or no natural person controls through ownership, identify who controls the company in other ways.

items.label: Step 3: senior management
items.detail: If no one is found at steps 1 or 2, identify the natural person holding a senior management position.

cards.question: A walk-in customer with no account at the Penang branch buys three bank drafts on the same morning: RM9,000, RM8,500 and RM9,000, all for the same payee. What does paragraph 14A.1 require?
options: No CDD, because each transaction is below RM25,000
CDD, because linked occasional transactions in a day total RM25,000 or more
Only sanctions screening, because CDD is for account holders
CDD only if the customer pays for the drafts in cash
cards.explanation: Paragraph 14A.1(e) covers occasional transactions of RM25,000 and above, including several transactions in a day that appear to be linked. Here they total RM26,500 for one payee on one morning. Splitting amounts to avoid a threshold may also be structuring, an offence under section 4A of AMLA.

cards.title: What standard CDD collects
cards.body:
**Individuals and beneficial owners (paragraph 14A.9.1)**: full name; NRIC, passport or other official document number; residential and mailing address; date of birth; nationality; occupation type; employer or nature of business; contact number; and purpose of the transaction. The bank must then verify identity using reliable, independent sources.

**Legal persons (paragraphs 14A.9.3 to 14A.9.7)**: understand the business and its ownership and control structure; obtain name, legal form and proof of existence, the powers that bind it, senior management names and the registered and business address; verify who is authorised to act; and identify beneficial owners. Where there is doubt, check the information with the Companies Commission of Malaysia, Labuan FSA or another relevant authority.

**Legal arrangements such as trusts**: identify the settlor, trustees, any protector, the beneficiaries or class, and anyone else with ultimate effective control.

**Timing (paragraph 14A.8)**: verify before or during the opening of the relationship.

cards.title: Onboarding a company, in BNM's order
cards.prompt: Put the onboarding steps for a new corporate customer in a sensible order.
steps: Screen the company, its directors and known owners against the Domestic List and UN lists
Collect the company's legal documents, registered address and the powers that bind it
Verify the identity and authority of the person acting for the company
Work through the beneficial owner cascade: ownership, then other control, then senior management
Assign a risk rating and decide between standard and enhanced CDD
Obtain senior management approval if enhanced CDD applies, then open the account

cards.title: Standard, enhanced or stop?
cards.prompt: Sort each onboarding situation into the action BNM's rules point to.

items.text: Salaried local teacher opening a savings account, documents verified
Customer from a country the FATF has called on members to apply enhanced measures to
Foreign PEP opening a premium current account
Company whose owners refuse to be identified after repeated requests
Domestic PEP assessed by the bank as higher risk
Applicant whose NRIC photo does not match the person at the counter
Listed company on Bursa Malaysia opening an operating account
Cash-intensive business with large unexplained deposits planned

lines.text: Update: the director's father-in-law is a senior official in a state government. Does that make the director a PEP?
Not the director himself. But BNM's PEP rules cover family members, and a spouse's parent is on BNM's family list. So the director is a family member of a domestic PEP.
For domestic PEPs and their families, BNM wants a risk assessment. Enhanced CDD is required if the relationship is assessed as higher risk.
And the Labuan owners are still 'confidential'.
Then we may never reach the PEP question. Let's decide this properly.

cards.title: Tebrau Freight: open, escalate or decline?
cards.situation: Tebrau Freight's lawyer still refuses to name the owners of the Labuan company that holds 70 per cent. One director is the son-in-law of a senior state official. The company wants the account active by Friday for a large shipment and offers to sign a letter promising the owners are 'reputable'. Kavitha must recommend a course of action to her manager.

choices.text: Accept the signed letter as enough for beneficial ownership and open the account by Friday.
choices.outcome: Poor. A letter of comfort does not identify or verify the natural persons behind the 70 per cent stake. Paragraph 14A.9.6 requires identification and reasonable verification. HSBC Bank Malaysia was penalised in 2025 for beneficial owner failures.

choices.text: Open the account, rate it high risk and monitor it closely until the owners are disclosed.
choices.outcome: Partly right on risk, but monitoring cannot replace CDD that was never completed. Paragraph 14A.16 says if CDD cannot be completed the bank must not open the account.

choices.text: Explain the bank cannot open without identifying the owners; if they still refuse, do not open and refer to compliance to consider an STR.
choices.outcome: Best. This follows paragraph 14A.16: no account without completed CDD, and the bank must consider an STR. If the owners are disclosed, the PEP family link is assessed for enhanced CDD.

choices.text: Open the account in the 30 per cent shareholder's personal name instead, as he is fully identified.
choices.outcome: Poor. This disguises who the real customer is, and AMLA forbids accounts in a false or incorrect name. It may also be a step towards tipping off or facilitating laundering.

cards.back: Someone who is or was entrusted with a prominent public function by a foreign country. Enhanced CDD and enhanced ongoing due diligence always apply.
Someone who is or was entrusted with a prominent public function in Malaysia, including federal, state and local government. The bank assesses the risk; enhanced measures apply if higher risk.
A member of senior management of an international organisation, such as a director or board member. Treated like a domestic PEP: risk-assessed.
BNM lists parent, sibling, spouse, child and spouse's parent, by blood, marriage or non-biological relationship.
People closely connected to a PEP socially or professionally, such as business partners, staff on the PEP's payroll or close friends.
BNM asks the bank to weigh the informal influence the person may still have and whether old and new roles link to the same matters. There is no automatic expiry date.

cards.title: Enhanced CDD: what BNM requires at minimum
cards.caption: Paragraphs 14A.12, 14A.13.5 and 15. Foreign PEPs always need these measures; domestic and international organisation PEPs need them when assessed as higher risk.

items.label: Information
items.left: Standard CDD details plus extra data on the customer and beneficial owner
items.right: Same, for every PEP subject to enhanced CDD

items.label: Source of money
items.left: Enquire on source of wealth or source of funds
items.right: Both source of wealth and source of funds

items.label: Approval
items.left: Senior management approval before opening or continuing

items.label: Monitoring
items.left: Enhanced ongoing due diligence: more controls, selected patterns

cards.question: A low-risk customer cannot produce her proof of address at account opening. Under BNM's delayed verification rules, what is the longest the bank may normally take to complete verification?
options: Thirty calendar days
Five working days
Ten working days, unless BNM specifies another period
Until the next periodic CDD review
cards.explanation: Paragraph 14A.10.7 says 'as soon as reasonably practicable' must not exceed ten working days or another period BNM specifies. Delayed verification is guidance-based flexibility only for low risk, with no suspicion, where the delay is essential and the risk is managed.

cards.title: Real case: HSBC Bank Malaysia and beneficial owners (BNM, 2025)
cards.body:
On 13 March 2025 BNM imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM324,000** on HSBC Bank Malaysia Berhad for failing to meet CDD requirements, citing paragraphs 14A.1(h), 14A.3(c) and 14A.9.6 of the 2019 policy document: identifying and taking reasonable measures to verify the natural persons who are a customer's **beneficial owners**.

BNM found the gaps in an on-site examination, which revealed a **lack of understanding of the beneficial owner requirements**. The bank responded by strengthening compliance monitoring and giving staff refresher training on beneficial ownership. BNM weighed the lack of reasonable care, the bank's past compliance record and its remedial actions.

**The lesson:** beneficial ownership is not a form-filling exercise. If staff cannot work the cascade, the bank cannot see who really controls its customers.

cards.title: Real case: Bank Pembangunan Malaysia (BNM, 2025)
cards.body:
BNM's published list of enforcement actions shows that on 14 February 2025 it imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM229,500** on Bank Pembangunan Malaysia Berhad, a development financial institution, for **failure to conduct customer due diligence**. The provisions cited were paragraphs 14A.3(c) and 14A.9.6 of the 2019 policy document, the same beneficial owner requirements as in the HSBC case.

BNM records that the institution took remedial steps to prevent recurrence.

**The lesson:** two banks in one quarter were penalised for the same paragraph. Beneficial ownership on corporate accounts is a known examination focus, so expect your files to be sampled.

cards.title: Relying on introducers and other banks
cards.body:
BNM lets a bank rely on a third party for CDD, but with firm limits (paragraph 16):

- **Responsibility stays with your bank.** Reliance never moves accountability.
- You must be able to get the CDD information **immediately**, and be satisfied the third party is regulated and keeps records.
- You must **not** rely on third parties located in higher-risk countries.
- You may **never** rely on a third party for **ongoing** due diligence; that is always your job.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: CDD is triggered by new relationships, occasional or cash transactions of RM25,000 or more, any suspicion, and doubts about earlier data.
Beneficial owners are found by a cascade: more than 25% ownership, then control by other means, then senior management.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not open or continue the relationship, and consider an STR.
Enhanced CDD means more information, source of wealth or funds (both for PEPs) and senior management approval (head office for PEPs).
Foreign PEPs always get enhanced CDD; domestic and international organisation PEPs are risk-assessed, and family includes a spouse's parent.
Delayed verification is for low-risk cases only and normally may not exceed ten working days.

cards.prompt: Pick a corporate customer file you know. Could you name its beneficial owners and explain which step of BNM's cascade you used to find them? What would you need to check?

quiz.question: At what amount must a bank carry out CDD on an occasional cash transaction under paragraph 14A.1?
options: RM25,000 and above
RM3,000 and above
RM10,000 and above
RM50,000 and above only
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14A.1(e) and (f) set RM25,000 and above for occasional and cash transactions. RM3,000 and RM10,000 appear in the specific CDD rules for wire transfers and money-changing.

quiz.question: A company's shareholders are Aminah with 20%, Boon with 26% and a foundation with 54% whose controllers are unclear. Applying step 1 of BNM's cascade, who must be identified at minimum?
options: Aminah and Boon, because both individuals hold more than 15% each, and the foundation can be ignored
Only the foundation, because it has the largest stake
Nobody, because no individual holds a majority stake
Boon, because he holds more than 25%, and then the foundation's controllers must be explored
quiz.explanation: Step 1 requires at least directors and shareholders with more than 25% equity. Boon qualifies. Where doubt remains about who controls through the foundation, step 2 looks at control by other means.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT among the minimum items BNM requires for identifying an individual customer under standard CDD?
options: Date of birth
Monthly income figure
Nationality
Purpose of transaction
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14A.9.1 lists full name, ID number, address, date of birth, nationality, occupation type, employer or business, contact number and purpose of transaction. Income is often asked, but it is not on the minimum list.

quiz.question: A prospective customer refuses to explain the purpose of a new business account or name its owners. What does paragraph 14A.16 require?
options: Do not open the account, and consider lodging an STR
Open the account and rate the customer as high risk
Open the account with lower transaction limits
Ask a senior manager to approve an exception to the CDD process
quiz.explanation: If CDD cannot be completed, the bank must not open the account or perform the transaction, and must consider an STR. Risk ratings and limits cannot replace incomplete CDD.

quiz.question: Kavitha learns that a new customer's mother is a federal deputy minister. Under BNM's policy document, what is the customer?
options: A foreign PEP, requiring enhanced CDD in every case and head office approval
Not covered, because PEP rules apply only to the office holder
A family member of a domestic PEP, requiring a risk assessment
A close associate, to whom PEP rules never apply
quiz.explanation: BNM's PEP rules apply to family members, including children. For domestic PEPs the bank assesses risk and applies enhanced CDD if the relationship is higher risk.

quiz.question: For a PEP who requires enhanced CDD, what must the bank obtain about the customer's money?
options: Source of funds only, for the first transaction
Both source of wealth and source of funds
Source of wealth only, at the first review
Either source, at the relationship manager's choice
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14A.12.1(c) asks the bank to enquire on source of wealth or funds for higher-risk customers, and says for PEPs both must be obtained.

quiz.question: Who must approve a new business relationship with a PEP that requires enhanced CDD?
options: The branch manager where the account is opened
The board of directors at its next meeting
The relationship manager's direct supervisor
Senior management at the bank's head office
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14A.12.1(d) requires senior management approval before establishing or continuing a higher-risk relationship, and for PEPs that means senior management at head office.

quiz.question: A bank wants to rely on an overseas introducer to perform CDD on new customers. Which arrangement does BNM prohibit?
options: Relying on a regulated third party in the same financial group
Relying on a third party located in a higher-risk country
Obtaining written confirmation that CDD has been done
Getting an attestation that the third party keeps records
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 16.4 prohibits reliance on third parties in higher-risk countries. Group reliance, written confirmations and attestations are all allowed or expected under paragraph 16.

quiz.question: A former foreign head of state left office three years ago but still chairs his party's funding committee. The RM wants to drop his PEP status. What should guide the decision?
options: A fixed rule in BNM's policy document that PEP status ends one year after the person leaves office
Whether the customer signs a declaration that he is no longer a PEP
Whether his account balance has fallen below the bank's PEP threshold
His remaining informal influence and whether old and new roles link to the same matters
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 15.4.1 tells banks to weigh the influence the person can still exercise and whether previous and current functions are linked. There is no automatic time limit.

quiz.question: HSBC Bank Malaysia was penalised RM324,000 in 2025. Which requirement did the breach concern?
options: Identifying and verifying customers' beneficial owners
Submitting cash threshold reports on time
Freezing funds of specified entities on the Domestic List immediately
Notifying FIED of a new Compliance Officer
quiz.explanation: BNM cited paragraphs 14A.1(h), 14A.3(c) and 14A.9.6, the beneficial owner requirements, and found a lack of understanding of them during an on-site examination.

sessions.title: Suspicion, STRs, Cash Threshold Reports and Tipping Off
sessions.summary: Escalate suspicion through the internal chain so the Compliance Officer can report promptly to FIED, file cash threshold reports correctly and never tip off a customer.
objectives: Describe the internal STR chain and the deadline for submission to FIED
Apply the RM25,000 cash threshold reporting rules and the five-working-day deadline
Recognise red flags from BNM's examples
Avoid tipping off and explain the protection for good-faith reporters

cards.title: Deposits from four states
cards.setting: Seri Merbau Bank, Penang George Town branch. 11:40 am.

lines.text: Here's the customer who asked whether we 'tell the government'. A student account, opened last year. Quiet until two months ago.
Since then: cash deposits through deposit machines in Kedah, Perak, Selangor and Johor, most between RM20,000 and RM24,000 a day, then fast transfers out to many different people.
Just under RM25,000 each day. Someone knows where the cash threshold sits.
The teller wants to know two things: should she report, and what does she say if he asks again?
Good questions. One is about the reporting chain, the other is about tipping off. Get either wrong and the bank, or the teller, is in trouble.
Stage three: the Signal Tower. Let's learn to send the right signal, to the right place, without warning anyone.

cards.title: How a suspicion becomes a report to FIED

scenes.heading: Someone notices
scenes.narration: Any employee who sees a transaction or activity that seems unusual, has no clear economic purpose, looks illegal or may involve crime proceeds raises an internal report. Attempted and proposed transactions count, and there is no minimum amount.

scenes.heading: The branch channel
scenes.narration: At a branch, the internal report goes to the designated branch compliance officer, who channels it to the Compliance Officer at head office. Head office staff report straight to the Compliance Officer.

scenes.heading: The Compliance Officer decides
scenes.narration: The Compliance Officer evaluates the grounds for suspicion. If there are no reasonable grounds, the decision and the supporting documents are recorded and filed.

scenes.heading: Prompt submission
scenes.narration: Once the suspicion is confirmed, the Compliance Officer submits the STR to FIED through the Financial Intelligence System, FINS, within the next working day.

scenes.heading: Secrecy throughout
scenes.narration: Reports and related information are kept strictly confidential. The bank answers FIED's follow-up requests promptly, and the customer is never told.

cards.title: The internal STR chain at Seri Merbau Bank
cards.caption: Paragraphs 22.1 to 22.4 of BNM's policy document. The Compliance Officer has sole discretion and independence to report.

items.label: Employee raises an internal report
items.detail: Facts, dates, amounts and why it looks suspicious. No investigation, no confrontation.

items.label: Branch compliance officer
items.detail: Channels every branch report to head office securely and confidentially.

items.label: Compliance Officer evaluates
items.detail: Within the review period set in the bank's policy; documents a decision not to report.

items.label: STR to FIED via FINS
items.detail: Within the next working day after the Compliance Officer establishes suspicion.

items.label: Follow-up and records
items.detail: Answer FIED's requests promptly; keep a complete file of all internal reports.

cards.title: Red flag or ordinary banking?
cards.prompt: Sort each observation. Red flags are triggers to escalate, not proof of crime.

items.text: Many cash deposits via machines in different states, each just under RM25,000
A retiree with no stated income receives frequent transfers from dozens of strangers
Large deposit into a new company account withdrawn within two days
Customer is accompanied by a third party who gives instructions and holds her documents
Several unrelated applicants share one mobile number and address
Monthly salary credit followed by usual bill payments
A hardware shop banks its weekend takings every Monday, in line with its profile
A customer pays her credit card bill in full from her own savings account

cards.question: Kenji deposits RM20,000 in cash in the morning and withdraws RM10,000 in cash from the same account that afternoon. What does the cash threshold rule require?
options: Nothing, because the net cash movement is only RM10,000
A cash threshold report, because the cash amounts are aggregated to RM30,000
A suspicious transaction report, because deposits and withdrawals on one day are always suspicious
A cash threshold report only if each transaction was RM25,000 or more
cards.explanation: Paragraph 21.3.2 forbids offsetting. Deposits and withdrawals in cash on the same account in a day are added together, so RM20,000 plus RM10,000 is RM30,000, above the RM25,000 threshold. A CTR is not an STR, and it never removes the duty to file an STR if there is suspicion.

cards.title: Cash threshold reports in brief
cards.body:
BNM requires banks to report cash transactions to FIED once they reach the threshold (paragraph 21):

- **What counts as cash:** physical notes and coins in any currency, and bearer negotiable instruments such as traveller's cheques or money orders. Bank drafts, ordinary cheques, electronic transfers and fixed deposit renewals do not count.
- **Threshold:** single or multiple cash transactions in the same account in one day totalling **RM25,000 or more**, including cash withdrawals and over-the-counter cash contra between accounts.
- **No offsetting:** deposits and withdrawals are added, not netted.
- **Deadline:** submit through FINS within **five working days** of the transaction, with complete and accurate information.
- **Not a substitute:** filing a CTR never discharges the separate duty to submit an STR.

Splitting cash to stay under the threshold may be **structuring**, an offence under section 4A of AMLA.

cards.title: STR and CTR side by side

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect
items.right: Cash of RM25,000 or more, same account, one day

items.label: Deadline
items.left: Next working day after suspicion is established
items.right: Within five working days of the transaction

items.label: Customer told?
items.left: Never: tipping off is an offence
items.right: Not disclosed: the same confidentiality applies

cards.title: 'Will you report me?'
cards.setting: Penang branch counter, two days later. 3:15 pm.

lines.text: The student is back with another bag of cash. He leans towards the teller, Mei Ling, and lowers his voice.
(watching from the back office) Mei Ling already filed an internal report yesterday. I passed it to Nurul this morning.
'Just tell me,' the customer says. 'Did someone report my account? My friend said banks do that.'
(on Daniel's phone) Whatever she says now matters. A wrong sentence could be a crime under section 14A.

cards.title: The teller's answer
cards.situation: Mei Ling's customer asks directly whether his account has been reported. An internal report is already with the Compliance Officer. The queue is long, the customer is getting loud, and Mei Ling wants to calm him down. What should she do?

choices.text: Reassure him: 'Don't worry, nothing has been reported, it's just a routine check.'
choices.outcome: Poor. Lying invites follow-up questions and may still signal that something is going on. She should not discuss reports at all, true or false.

choices.text: Tell him honestly that compliance is looking at his deposits, so he can explain them.
choices.outcome: Poor. Disclosing that a report is proposed or made is tipping off under section 14A of AMLA, punishable by a fine of up to RM3 million or up to five years' prison, or both.

choices.text: Process his transaction in line with normal procedure, give a neutral answer that the bank does not discuss internal processes, and tell Daniel what was said.
choices.outcome: Best. She neither confirms nor denies, follows procedure, and passes the new information up the chain. The Compliance Officer can add it to the STR.

choices.text: Refuse the deposit and ask him to leave, saying the bank no longer wants his business.
choices.outcome: Partly understandable, but a sudden refusal at this moment may itself signal suspicion. Decisions to exit must come from compliance, timed so they do not tip off the customer.

cards.title: When disclosure is allowed (AMLA s14A(3))
cards.prompt: Match each situation to how section 14A treats it.

pairs.left: Compliance Officer sends the STR to FIED
pairs.right: Allowed: done in the course of duties under AMLA.

pairs.left: Warning a related Malaysian financial firm about a risky customer
pairs.right: Allowed within the conditions of s14A(3)(b) and the bank's controls.

pairs.left: A director gives the bank's supervisor information in the course of duty
Sharing report details with written authorisation of FIED's Director
pairs.right: Allowed: the bank applies in writing, with justification and safeguards.

pairs.left: Telling the customer's accountant that an STR was lodged
pairs.right: Not allowed: tipping off, an offence for the person who discloses.

pairs.left: A colleague who hears about the STR and posts it in a chat group
pairs.right: Not allowed: further disclosure is also an offence under s14A(2).

cards.question: After reviewing an internal report from Penang, Nurul concludes there are no reasonable grounds for suspicion. What must she do?
options: Delete the internal report so it cannot be misread later
Submit an STR anyway, because every internal report must reach FIED
Document and file her decision with the supporting documents
Return the report to the branch and ask Daniel to decide
cards.explanation: Paragraph 22.2.3 requires the Compliance Officer to document and file a decision not to report, with supporting documents, and paragraph 22.4 requires a complete file of all internal reports, submitted or not, available to supervisors on request.

cards.title: Real case: AmBank and late cash threshold reports (BNM, 2026)
cards.body:
On 10 September 2026 BNM imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM276,000** on AmBank (M) Berhad for failing to submit cash threshold reports promptly, in breach of paragraph 21.4.3 of the policy documents in force over the period.

The bank found the breaches itself, in a review of its transaction and regulatory reporting records: CTRs for multiple transactions had not been sent to BNM. BNM put this down to **lapses in technology implementation arising from inadequate oversight of system changes**. The bank submitted the omitted reports and strengthened its procedures, systems and oversight.

BNM counted **self-reporting** and effective remediation in its assessment, alongside the lack of reasonable care.

**The lesson:** a system change can silently break a reporting duty. Test reports after every change, and report problems early.

cards.title: Reporting numbers to remember
cards.caption: From paragraphs 21 and 22 of BNM's policy document.

items.label: STR threshold
items.detail: Suspicion triggers an STR regardless of amount, including attempted or proposed transactions.

items.label: STR deadline
items.detail: From the date the Compliance Officer establishes the suspicion.

items.label: CTR threshold
items.detail: Cash in the same account in one day, deposits and withdrawals added together.

items.label: CTR deadline
items.detail: From the date of the transaction, through FINS.

cards.front: Am I protected if I report in good faith?
cards.back: Yes. AMLA section 24 bars civil, criminal or disciplinary proceedings over information given in a report, unless it was given in bad faith.

cards.front: Do I need proof before raising a report?
cards.back: No. Reason to suspect is enough. Investigating or questioning the customer to 'be sure' risks tipping off.

cards.front: Can CDD itself tip off the customer?
cards.back: It can. If pursuing CDD would tip off a suspected customer, the bank may stop CDD, record why, and file an STR immediately (paragraph 14A.17).

cards.front: Does an STR have to wait for the transaction to finish?
cards.back: No. Attempted and proposed transactions are reportable, and the bank can file a fresh or updated STR when new suspicion arises.
The Compliance Officer, who under BNM's rules has sole discretion and independence to report. Your job is to escalate, not to decide.

cards.title: Writing an internal report that helps
cards.body:
BNM asks that STRs explain what gave rise to doubt. Your internal report is the raw material, so:

- State **facts**: dates, amounts, channels, accounts and people involved.
- Say **why** it looked unusual against what you know of the customer.
- Note anything the customer **said**, word for word if you can.
- Do **not** speculate about crimes or label the customer.
- Send it only through the bank's secure channel, never by personal chat.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Suspicion of any amount, including attempted or proposed transactions, must be escalated: employee, branch compliance officer, then the Compliance Officer.
The Compliance Officer submits STRs to FIED via FINS within the next working day after establishing suspicion, and documents decisions not to file.
Cash of RM25,000 or more in one account in a day is reported as a CTR within five working days; deposits and withdrawals are added, not netted.
Tipping off is an offence under section 14A of AMLA: up to RM3 million, five years' prison, or both.
Good-faith reporters are protected by section 24 of AMLA.

cards.prompt: If a customer asked you tomorrow whether the bank had 'reported' them, what exact words would you use? Write them down and check them against the bank's procedure.

quiz.question: A teller at the Penang branch suspects a deposit. Under BNM's reporting mechanism, where does her internal report go first?
options: Directly to FIED through FINS
To the designated branch compliance officer
To the branch manager for approval before anything else
To the customer's relationship manager
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 22.2.1 makes the branch compliance officer responsible for channelling all internal reports from branch staff to the Compliance Officer at head office.

quiz.question: Nurul establishes suspicion on a case on Tuesday. By when must the STR reach FIED?
options: Within five working days
Within ten working days
By the end of the calendar month
Within the next working day
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 22.2.6 requires submission within the next working day from the date the Compliance Officer establishes the suspicion. Five working days is the CTR deadline.

quiz.question: A customer tries to transfer RM800 to a person he says is 'supporting fighters overseas', then cancels when asked for details. What should staff do?
options: Nothing, because the transfer did not go through
Escalate an internal report: attempted transactions of any amount are reportable
Nothing, because the amount is below every threshold
Report it only if he tries again later with a larger amount that crosses a reporting threshold
quiz.explanation: Section 14 of AMLA covers attempted and proposed transactions, including links to terrorism, and BNM requires STRs regardless of amount.

quiz.question: Which of these counts as cash for a cash threshold report?
options: A bank draft issued against an account
An online transfer between two accounts of the same customer
A fixed deposit renewed on maturity
Traveller's cheques exchanged over the counter
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 21.2.1 includes physical currency and bearer negotiable instruments such as traveller's cheques, but excludes bank drafts, cheques, electronic transfers and fixed deposit rollovers.

quiz.question: A customer asks Mei Ling whether 'someone reported' his account. An internal report has been raised. Which answer is safest?
options: A neutral reply that the bank does not discuss internal processes, then tell the branch compliance officer
Confirm that compliance is reviewing the account so that he has a fair chance to explain the deposits before any report
Say no report exists, to calm him down
Tell him to ask the Compliance Officer directly by email
quiz.explanation: Disclosing that a report is proposed or made is tipping off under section 14A of AMLA. A neutral reply avoids both disclosure and false reassurance, and the new information goes up the chain.

quiz.question: What is the maximum penalty for tipping off under section 14A of AMLA?
options: A fine of up to RM1 million only
Up to fifteen years' prison and a fine of at least RM5 million
A fine of up to RM3 million or up to five years' prison, or both
A written reprimand from BNM
quiz.explanation: Section 14A sets a fine not exceeding RM3 million or imprisonment up to five years, or both. Fifteen years and RM5 million relate to the money laundering offence itself.

quiz.question: While doing CDD on a walk-in customer, Daniel forms a suspicion and believes further questions would tip the customer off. What does paragraph 14A.17 allow?
options: Finish all CDD questions first, and only then decide on an STR
Ask the customer to come back with a lawyer
Stop the CDD, record why, and file an STR immediately
Refer the customer to another bank without comment
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14A.17.1 permits the bank not to pursue CDD where it would tip off a suspected customer, provided it documents the reason and immediately files an STR.

quiz.question: A teller who filed an internal report in good faith worries the customer will sue her. What does AMLA say?
options: Section 24 bars civil, criminal or disciplinary proceedings unless the report was in bad faith
She is protected only if the STR leads to a conviction
She is protected only if the Compliance Officer eventually files an STR with FIED and it leads to a conviction
She has no protection; only the bank is protected
quiz.explanation: Section 24(1) protects people who disclose or supply information in a report from civil, criminal or disciplinary proceedings, unless it was in bad faith.

quiz.question: AmBank (M) Berhad was penalised RM276,000 in 2026 for late cash threshold reports. What did BNM say caused the lapses?
options: Tellers who deliberately split customers' cash deposits to stay under the threshold
A Compliance Officer who refused to submit the reports
Customers who gave false identity documents at the counter
Technology implementation lapses from inadequate oversight of system changes
quiz.explanation: BNM's notice attributed the missed CTRs to lapses in technology implementation arising from inadequate oversight of system changes. The bank found the breaches itself and self-reported.

quiz.question: A customer deposits RM15,000 cash in the morning and RM12,000 cash in the afternoon into the same account. No suspicion arises. What does the bank file?
options: Nothing, because each deposit is below RM25,000
A cash threshold report within five working days
A suspicious transaction report within one working day
Both a CTR and an STR, as always required
quiz.explanation: Multiple cash transactions in the same account in a day are aggregated. RM27,000 reaches the RM25,000 threshold, so a CTR is due within five working days. An STR is needed only if there is suspicion.

sessions.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions on Terrorism and Proliferation Financing
sessions.summary: Screen against the Domestic and UN lists without delay, resolve potential matches, freeze, block or reject, and report to FIED and the police under BNM's paragraphs 27 to 29.
objectives: Explain the TF, PF and other UN sanctions regimes and who authorises dealings in frozen funds
Apply the screening, database and re-screening duties, including for dormant accounts
Respond correctly to a potential and a confirmed match
Learn from BNM's published TFS enforcement cases

cards.title: Friday, 4:50 pm: the Gazette
cards.setting: Sanctions screening desk, head office, Kuala Lumpur.

lines.text: Nurul, the Minister of Home Affairs has just added three names to the Domestic List. It's in the Gazette. It's ten to five on a Friday.
Then our sanctions database gets updated now, not on Monday. BNM's word is 'without delay'.
Re-screening the whole customer base too? Including dormant accounts?
Including dormant accounts. That's in the policy document.
First pass is done. One possible hit: a dormant account in Ipoh with a similar name and the same year of birth.
Welcome to the Frozen Vault, stage four. Possible matches, true matches, freezing and reporting. Let's work it through.

scenes.heading: Terrorism financing
scenes.narration: Paragraph 27 covers the UN lists on ISIL, Al-Qaida and the Taliban, plus Malaysia's own Domestic List declared by the Minister of Home Affairs. People on these lists are specified entities.

scenes.heading: Proliferation financing
scenes.narration: Paragraph 28 covers UN designations on weapons of mass destruction, given effect in Malaysia through the Strategic Trade Act 2010. Here the Strategic Trade Controller authorises any dealing with frozen funds.

scenes.heading: Other UN regimes
scenes.narration: Paragraph 29 covers other UN Security Council sanctions, for example those aimed at armed conflict, given effect through regulations under the Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009.

scenes.heading: Without delay
scenes.narration: For each regime the bank keeps its sanctions database current as soon as a listing is published, screens all customers and transactions, and freezes or blocks immediately on a confirmed match.

scenes.heading: Report and keep reporting
scenes.narration: The bank reports positive matches at once, keeps reporting changes to frozen funds, and files suspicious transaction reports on related and attempted transactions.

cards.title: Terrorism financing and proliferation financing TFS

items.label: Lists
items.left: UN ISIL/Al-Qaida/Taliban lists and the Domestic List
items.right: UN proliferation designations under the Strategic Trade Act

items.label: Authority for dealings and exemptions
items.left: Minister of Home Affairs, in writing

items.label: Immediate match report goes to
items.left: FIED and the Inspector-General of Police

items.label: Also required
items.left: Periodic reports on frozen funds; STRs on related or attempted transactions
items.right: Periodic reports on frozen funds; STRs on related or attempted transactions

cards.title: The screening loop
cards.caption: Screening applies to every customer and transaction, regardless of CDD thresholds or product features.

items.label: New listing published
items.detail: UN website or Malaysian Gazette.

items.label: Update the database without delay
items.detail: Accessible to head office, branches and relevant agents.

items.label: Screen the whole customer base
items.detail: Including dormant accounts, potential customers and transactions.

items.label: Resolve potential matches
items.detail: Further inquiries to separate true matches from false positives.

items.label: Act and report
items.detail: Freeze, block or reject; report; keep records of screening.

cards.question: Seri Merbau Bank confirms that a current account holder is a specified entity on the Domestic List. Besides freezing the funds, who must it report to immediately?
options: FIED and the Inspector-General of Police
Only the Ministry of Home Affairs
Only the bank's board risk committee
The customer, so that he can apply for an exemption
cards.explanation: Paragraph 27.7.1 requires an immediate report to FIED and the Inspector-General of Police, using the template in Appendix 8a, once the bank finds it holds funds of a specified entity or related party. The bank may tell the person they can apply to the Minister for an exemption, but that is not the report.

cards.title: Screening duties in detail
cards.body:
For each regime, BNM's policy document sets the same core duties:

- **Keep a sanctions database** for the UN list and, for terrorism, the Domestic List; update it **without delay** when a listing is published, and keep names on it until formal delisting.
- **Screen existing, potential and new customers**, as part of CDD and ongoing due diligence, and screen transactions. There is **no threshold**.
- **Collect the minimum data points** to screen: full name, NRIC or passport number and date of birth.
- **Re-screen the entire customer database**, including dormant accounts, whenever a new designation is published.
- **Deal with false positives**: make further inquiries with the customer, counterparty or credible sources. For common names the bank may ask FIED.
- **Look at related parties**: people acting for a listed person, or holding funds owned or controlled by one, and analyse past transactions.
- **Keep records** of all screening and make them available to supervisors.

cards.title: A confirmed match on the Domestic List
cards.prompt: Put Farid's actions in order once the Ipoh account turns out to be a true match.
steps: Confirm the match through further inquiries and identification documents
Freeze the funds and block transactions immediately and without delay
Report at once to FIED and the Inspector-General of Police using the prescribed form
Submit a suspicious transaction report on the account and any related or attempted transactions
Analyse past transactions and look for related parties
Report changes to the frozen funds at the intervals BNM specifies

cards.title: Frozen funds: what can happen?
cards.prompt: Sort each request about a frozen terrorism-related account.

items.text: Crediting interest or dividends to the frozen account, which stay frozen
Telling the listed person they may apply to the Minister for a basic expenses exemption
Paying the listed person's medical bills from the frozen balance
A relative asks to withdraw part of the balance on the person's behalf
Opening a new account for a potential customer who is a positive name match
Waiting until Monday to freeze because the screening team has gone home
Unfreezing because the customer says the listing is a mistake

lines.text: The Ipoh account: the name matches a listed person and the birth year matches. But our NRIC number for the customer doesn't fit the listing's details.
So it's a potential match, not yet a true match. What does BNM say we do with potential matches?
Make further inquiries: documents, the counterparty, credible sources. And for common names we can query FIED.
(joining) The Ipoh branch manager wants to call the customer and ask if he's 'that person'.
Careful. Let's decide how to resolve this without either freezing an innocent person for weeks or tipping off a real one.

cards.title: Resolving the Ipoh potential match
cards.situation: A dormant account in Ipoh matches the name and birth year of a person newly added to the Domestic List, but the NRIC number held by the bank differs from the details in the listing. The account holds about RM48,000. It is Saturday. What should the bank do?

choices.text: Treat it as a false positive straight away, because the NRIC number differs, and close the alert.
choices.outcome: Poor. A differing number is useful, but BNM requires the bank to ascertain whether a potential match is a true match through further inquiries. Closing it on one data point, without records, is how screening breaches happen.

choices.text: Keep the alert open, make further inquiries quickly through compliance, query FIED on the common name, and freeze and report at once if it is confirmed.
choices.outcome: Best. The bank resolves the match promptly with evidence, can query FIED for similar or common names, and is ready to freeze and report immediately on confirmation. Every step is recorded.

choices.text: Ask the branch manager to phone the customer and ask whether he is the listed person.
choices.outcome: Poor. If the customer is the listed person, this may warn him and lead to the funds moving. Inquiries should be made through controlled channels set by compliance.

choices.text: Freeze and report it as a confirmed match now, and sort out the details next week.
choices.outcome: Partly right on speed, but reporting an unconfirmed match as confirmed may harm an innocent customer. The policy document asks the bank to ascertain true matches; fast, documented inquiries come first.

cards.back: Names declared as specified entities by the Minister of Home Affairs under section 66B of AMLA and published in the Gazette.
Persons designated by the UN Security Council or its sanctions committees; for terrorism they are deemed specified entities under section 66C of AMLA.
A person who holds funds owned or controlled by a listed person, or who acts on behalf of or at the direction of one.
A potential customer or customer confirmed as a listed person. Potential customers must be rejected; existing customers' funds frozen.
Lists of other countries. Banks may add them to the database; a positive match with one calls for an STR (paragraph 27.8.3).
Payments from frozen funds that need written authorisation from the Minister of Home Affairs, or for PF the Strategic Trade Controller.

cards.title: Real case: AEON Credit and a missed rejection (BNM, 2026)
cards.body:
On 6 April 2026 BNM imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM520,000** on AEON Credit Service (M) Berhad for breaching targeted financial sanctions requirements, citing paragraphs 27.6.1 and 27.6.2.

An on-site examination found that a specified entity on the **Domestic List** had been onboarded. The institution **failed to reject** the applicant despite a positive match, and there was a **delay in freezing** the account after the customer was confirmed as a specified entity.

BNM's notice put the breaches down to **lack of staff oversight and a gap in the standard operating procedure**. The remedy included an improved SOP and **refresher training** for relevant staff.

**The lesson:** a hit that is seen but not acted on is worse than no screening at all. Rejection and freezing must be immediate.

cards.title: Real cases: screening against outdated or skipped lists (BNM, 2025-2026)
cards.body:
**Standard Chartered Bank Malaysia Berhad, 2026.** BNM imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM132,000** on 10 June 2026 after an on-site examination found the bank had not updated its sanctions database **without delay** when the Domestic List was published, so screening ran against an outdated database. BNM noted that no specified entity was onboarded and no transaction facilitated.

**HSBC Bank Malaysia Berhad, 2025.** BNM's notice of 28 May 2025 described customers onboarded **without proper sanctions screening** because of staff oversight, ineffective maker-checker controls and inadequate systems, recurring after the first fix. Penalties for the screening breaches totalled about RM2.9 million across HSBC's two Malaysian banking entities.

**The lesson:** BNM penalised these breaches even though no listed person was found. The duty is the process itself.

cards.question: Under the proliferation financing sanctions, who must authorise payment of basic expenses from funds the bank has frozen?
options: The Minister of Home Affairs
The bank's Compliance Officer
The Strategic Trade Controller under the Strategic Trade Act 2010
The Inspector-General of Police
cards.explanation: Paragraph 28 points to the Strategic Trade Controller for any dealing with, and exemptions from, funds frozen under the PF sanctions. The Minister of Home Affairs plays that role for the terrorism-related lists under paragraph 27.

cards.title: TFS penalties published by BNM
cards.caption: Administrative monetary penalties from BNM's enforcement notices. Several cases involved no actual listed person: the failure was the process.

items.label: Zurich General Insurance, 2026
items.detail: Outdated database, unresolved matches, late freezing and late reporting to BNM.

items.label: AEON Credit Service, 2026
items.detail: Failed to reject a positive match; delayed freezing.

items.label: Standard Chartered Bank Malaysia, 2026
items.detail: Domestic List not updated without delay; screening against old data.

items.label: HSBC Malaysia entities, 2025
items.detail: New customers onboarded without proper sanctions screening, twice.

cards.title: Five habits for screening staff
cards.body:
- **Clock starts at publication.** Check the UN website and the Gazette routinely, not only when told.
- **Never clear a hit on one data point.** Use name, NRIC or passport number, date of birth and other details together, and record your reasoning.
- **Dormant means in scope.** Re-screen the whole base after each new listing.
- **Release nothing without paper.** Frozen funds stay frozen until delisting unless written authorisation is given.
- **Report twice:** the TFS match report and, where relevant, an STR.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Banks must keep sanctions databases current without delay and screen all customers and transactions, regardless of thresholds.
After each new listing, the whole customer base is re-screened, including dormant accounts.
On a confirmed match: freeze or block immediately, reject potential customers, report at once and file an STR on related or attempted transactions.
Terrorism-related matches go to FIED and the Inspector-General of Police; dealings need the Minister of Home Affairs' written authorisation.
Proliferation financing matches go to FIED; dealings and exemptions need the Strategic Trade Controller's written authorisation.

cards.prompt: Where in your daily work could a listed person or their front reach the bank: a new account, a payment, a guarantee, a trade document? What would you check, and who would you call?

quiz.question: Who declares the names on Malaysia's Domestic List of specified entities?
options: The Governor of Bank Negara Malaysia
The Attorney General
The Minister of Home Affairs
The Minister of Finance
quiz.explanation: The Domestic List is declared by the Minister of Home Affairs under section 66B of AMLA and published in the Gazette.

quiz.question: When must a bank update its sanctions database after a new UN designation is published?
options: Within five working days
At the next monthly list refresh
Without delay upon publication
When the customer next transacts
quiz.explanation: BNM requires the sanctions database to be updated and effected without delay upon publication. Standard Chartered Bank Malaysia was penalised in 2026 for not doing so for the Domestic List.

quiz.question: After a new listing, should Seri Merbau Bank re-screen dormant accounts?
options: Yes: the entire customer database, including dormant accounts, must be screened without delay
No: dormant accounts are screened only when they are reactivated
Only if the dormant account holds more than RM25,000
Only if the account was opened within the last six years and still holds a balance above RM25,000
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 27.4.4 requires screening of the entire customer database, including dormant accounts, without delay for any positive name match.

quiz.question: A potential new customer is a positive name match with the UN ISIL and Al-Qaida list. What must the bank do?
options: Open the account but freeze it immediately
Open the account and monitor it closely
Ask the customer for a written explanation before deciding
Reject the potential customer and report as required
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 27.6.2 requires the bank to reject a potential customer when there is a positive name match. AEON Credit was penalised in 2026 for failing to reject one.

quiz.question: A frozen account of a specified entity receives a dividend payment. What happens to it?
options: It must be returned to the payer immediately
It may be credited, but it remains frozen while the listing lasts
It may be paid out to the customer's family to cover their needs
It must be transferred to the Inspector-General of Police
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 27.6.5 allows frozen accounts to receive dividends, interest and other benefits, but they must stay frozen as long as the entity remains listed.

quiz.question: A listed person asks the bank to release frozen funds to pay rent and food. What may the bank do?
options: Tell him he may apply to the Minister of Home Affairs, and pay only on written authorisation
Pay basic expenses, since they are allowed automatically
Pay up to a small monthly limit set by the bank's Compliance Officer, recording each payment carefully in the file
Refuse to discuss exemptions in any circumstances
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 27.6.6 allows the bank to advise the person to apply to the Minister for basic and extraordinary expenditure exemptions; paragraph 27.6.7 says payment only follows written authorisation.

quiz.question: A customer is a positive match on a foreign country's unilateral sanctions list but not on the UN or Domestic lists. What does BNM's policy document require?
options: Freeze the funds and report to the police
